Hypothesis.summary: In elections where the impact on policy is greater, the relative influence of policy factors is greater than that of candidate characteristic factors.

c1.text: In elections where the impact on policy is greater, the relative influence of policy factors is greater than that of candidate characteristic factors.

c2.text: ⓐ is the proportion of voters who, when an opposing party's candidate is superior in personal characteristics, vote for that superior candidate.

c3.text: A greater relative influence of policy factors over candidate characteristic factors results in a lower defection rate ⓐ (and vice versa).

c4.text: In general, the president has a greater impact on policy than individual members of parliament.

h1.text: When presidential and parliamentary elections were held simultaneously, ⓐ was higher in the parliamentary election than in the presidential election.

h2.text: In simultaneous elections, the presidential election has a greater impact on policy than the parliamentary election.

a.note: From c4, the presidential election has greater policy impact than the parliamentary election; observing higher defection rate ⓐ in the parliamentary election confirms the hypothesis prediction and strengthens it.

h3.text: In the parliamentary election, ⓐ among progressive party supporters was lower when the president was from a conservative party compared to when the president was from a progressive party.

h4.text: The parliamentary election results conflict with the hypothesis.

h5.text: Progressive party supporters perceive the parliamentary election as having a greater policy impact when the sitting president is from a conservative party than when from a progressive party.

b.note: The naive inference rb1 (that lower defection ⓐ under an opposing president weakens the hypothesis) is undercut by h5: progressive voters perceive greater policy impact when the sitting president is from an opposing party, which actually aligns with the hypothesis.

h6.text: In the parliamentary election, ⓐ was lower when the majority party in parliament did not change compared to when it changed.

h7.text: When the majority party in parliament does not change, the parliamentary election has less impact on policy than when it changes.

h8.text: In elections where the impact on policy is smaller, the relative influence of policy factors is greater than that of candidate characteristic factors.

c.note: When the majority does not change, policy impact is smaller; observing lower ⓐ indicates greater influence of policy factors, which contradicts the hypothesis (h8). Thus the observation conflicts with and weakens rather than strengthens the hypothesis.
